questions.question: The first woman Prime Minister of India was _____.

questions.question: The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, after its introduction in the Lok Sabha, was examined by the _______.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Standing Committee on Home Affairs**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The **Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), 2023**, which seeks to replace the Indian Penal Code (IPC), 1860, was introduced in the Lok Sabha in August 2023.
 
• After its introduction, the BNSS, 2023, was referred to the **Standing Committee on Home Affairs** for detailed examination and recommendations.
 
• The Standing Committee on Home Affairs is responsible for addressing key legislative proposals and issues related to internal security, law, and order, as well as criminal justice reforms.
 
• The BNSS aims to modernize the criminal justice system in India by introducing reforms in criminal procedures and penal provisions to make them more citizen-friendly and efficient.
 
• The proposed changes include simplifying legal language, strengthening safeguards for citizens, and providing faster resolution of cases.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Standing Committee on External Affairs**

 
 
• This committee examines legislative and policy-related matters concerning **India's foreign relations**, diplomacy, and external security.
 
• It plays a crucial role in reviewing India's bilateral and multilateral engagements and provides recommendations on treaties, agreements, and foreign policies.
 
• The committee also evaluates the functioning of the Ministry of External Affairs and its affiliated bodies.
 
 
 
• **Standing Committee on Commerce**
 
 
• The Standing Committee on Commerce deals with issues related to **trade, commerce, and industries** in India.
 
• It examines legislative proposals, policies, and the functioning of the Ministry of Commerce and Industry.
 
• Key areas of focus include foreign trade, export promotion, industrial development, and e-commerce regulations.
 
 
 
• **Standing Committee on Railways**
 
 
• This committee examines matters related to the **Indian Railways**, including its infrastructure, operations, and services.
 
• It reviews legislative proposals and policies under the purview of the Ministry of Railways and suggests improvements for the development of the railway sector.
 
• It also evaluates passenger safety, freight services, and modernization initiatives.
 
 
 
• **Main Theme: Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023**
 
 
• The BNSS, 2023, is part of a comprehensive reform process aimed at replacing colonial-era laws such as the Indian Penal Code (IPC), the Criminal Procedure Code (CrPC), and the Indian Evidence Act.
 
• It emphasizes enhancing transparency, accountability, and efficiency in the criminal justice system.
 
• The proposed changes are designed to align the legal framework with contemporary needs and societal expectations in India.

questions.question: The Home Rule Movement in India, a key early 20th-century initiative advocating for self-government within the British Empire, drew significant inspiration from which of the following?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**The Irish Home Rule movement**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Home Rule Movement in India was inspired by the **Irish Home Rule Movement**, which advocated for self-government within the British Empire.
 
• Irish leaders like **Charles Stewart Parnell** and their methods of peaceful constitutional agitation influenced Indian leaders such as Annie Besant and Bal Gangadhar Tilak.
 
• Annie Besant, a key figure in the Indian Home Rule Movement, had previously been involved with Irish politics and brought her experience to India.
 
• The movement aimed to achieve **dominion status for India**, similar to Ireland’s demands, while staying within the framework of the British Empire.
 
• Two Home Rule Leagues were established in India in 1916 by **Annie Besant** and **Bal Gangadhar Tilak**, emphasizing the concept of self-rule inspired by Ireland’s struggle.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **The American Revolutionary War**

 
 
• The American Revolutionary War (1775–1783) led to the independence of the United States from British colonial rule.
 
• Although it served as a general inspiration for anti-imperial movements globally, it did not directly influence the Indian Home Rule Movement.
 
• The focus of the American Revolution was complete independence, whereas the Indian Home Rule Movement initially sought dominion status within the British Empire.
 
 
 
• **The Russian Revolution**
 
 
• The Russian Revolution of 1917 resulted in the overthrow of the Tsarist autocracy and the establishment of the Soviet Union.
 
• While the revolution inspired radical movements worldwide, it was not a direct influence on India’s Home Rule Movement, which followed constitutional and non-violent methods.
 
 
 
• **The Glorious Revolution**
 
 
• The Glorious Revolution (1688) in England resulted in the establishment of a constitutional monarchy and parliamentary supremacy.
 
• This event was significant in the history of constitutional development but had no direct relevance to the Home Rule Movement in India.
 
 
 
• **The Irish Home Rule Movement**
 
 
• The Irish Home Rule Movement served as a model for India’s Home Rule Movement in terms of strategies, goals, and organizational methods.
 
• It emphasized autonomy and self-government within the British Empire rather than complete independence.
 
• Indian leaders admired the Irish focus on constitutional methods and peaceful agitation, which they adapted to suit the Indian context.

questions.question: The main constitutional role of the Attorney General is to be the ______.

options.text: Comptroller and Auditor General of India
chief legal advisor to the Government of India

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**chief legal advisor to the Government of India**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Attorney General of India is the **chief legal advisor to the Government of India** as per Article 76 of the Indian Constitution.
 
• He/she is appointed by the President of India and holds office during the pleasure of the President.
 
• The Attorney General advises the government on legal matters and represents the government in the Supreme Court and other courts when required.
 
• The Attorney General has the right to participate in the proceedings of both Houses of Parliament but does not have the right to vote.
 
• He/she must be qualified to be appointed as a judge of the Supreme Court, i.e., must have been a judge of a High Court for five years, or an advocate in a High Court for ten years, or an eminent jurist.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Comptroller and Auditor General of India (CAG):**

 
 
• The CAG is an independent authority under Article 148 of the Constitution responsible for auditing the accounts of the Union and State governments.
 
• The CAG ensures transparency and accountability in the financial administration of the country.
 
• The CAG reports are submitted to the President or Governor and are then tabled in the Parliament or State Legislature.
 
 
 
• **Solicitor General of India:**
 
 
• The Solicitor General is the second-highest law officer of the country after the Attorney General.
 
• He/she assists the Attorney General in performing legal duties and also represents the government in courts when required.
 
• The Solicitor General is appointed by the government but is not a constitutional authority.
 
 
 
• **Election Commissioner:**
 
 
• The Election Commission of India is an autonomous constitutional authority responsible for administering election processes in India under Article 324.
 
• It ensures free and fair elections to the Parliament, State Legislatures, and the offices of the President and Vice-President.
 
• The Commission consists of the Chief Election Commissioner and other Election Commissioners.

questions.question: The main feature of the Northern Plain is its formation primarily by _________.

options.text: composed mainly of ancient igneous rocks
characterized by high plateaus and deep valleys

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Formed by rivers and alluvium**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Northern Plains of India are primarily formed by the deposition of sediments brought down by three major river systems: the Indus, the Ganga, and the Brahmaputra, as well as their tributaries.
 
• The process of alluvial deposition over millions of years has created this extensive plain, making it one of the most fertile regions in the world.
 
• This plain is characterized by rich, deep alluvial soils, which are ideal for agriculture, supporting crops such as wheat, rice, and sugarcane.
 
• The Northern Plain is divided into three sections: the Punjab Plains (formed by the Indus River and its tributaries), the Ganga Plains (formed by the Ganga River and its tributaries), and the Brahmaputra Plains (formed by the Brahmaputra River and its tributaries).
 
• Stretching from Punjab in the west to Assam in the east, these plains are a significant geographical feature of India, supporting a dense population and contributing immensely to the nation's economy.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Composed mainly of ancient igneous rocks:**

 
 
• This characteristic is typically associated with the Peninsular Plateau of India, not the Northern Plains.
 
• The Peninsular Plateau is a region made up of ancient crystalline rocks, primarily granite and basalt, which are some of the oldest rocks on Earth.
 
• It is known for its rugged terrain, hills, and rich mineral resources.
 
 
 
• **Characterized by high plateaus and deep valleys:**
 
 
• This description fits regions like the Western Ghats, Eastern Ghats, or other hilly terrains in India, not the flat and fertile Northern Plains.
 
• High plateaus, such as the Deccan Plateau, are elevated regions with relatively flat surfaces, and deep valleys are often formed by river erosion.
 
 
 
• **Dominated by coastal marshlands:**
 
 
• Coastal marshlands are found along the coastal regions of India, especially in areas like the Sundarbans in West Bengal or the Rann of Kutch in Gujarat.
 
• These areas are characterized by saline soils and are unsuitable for the types of agricultural practices seen in the Northern Plains.

questions.question: According to the 2011 Census, the second most spoken language in India after Hindi is _______.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Bengali**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• According to the 2011 Census, Bengali is the **second most spoken language in India**, with over 9.72 crore (97.2 million) speakers, making up approximately 8% of the total population.
 
• Bengali is the **official language of the state of West Bengal** and the union territory of the Andaman and Nicobar Islands.
 
• It is also widely spoken in the northeastern states of Tripura and Assam, especially in the Barak Valley region.
 
• Bengali is part of the **Indo-Aryan language family** and is known for its rich literary tradition, including works by Nobel laureate Rabindranath Tagore.
 
• Globally, Bengali is the fifth most spoken language, with a significant number of speakers in Bangladesh, where it is the national and official language.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Hindi**

 
 
• Hindi is the most spoken language in India, with over 52 crore (520 million) speakers, accounting for approximately 43.63% of the total population, as per the 2011 Census.
 
• It is one of the official languages of the Union Government and is widely spoken across northern and central India.
 
• Hindi belongs to the Indo-Aryan language family and serves as a lingua franca for many regions in India.
 
• It is written in the Devanagari script and has a rich literary and cultural heritage.
 
 
 
• **Urdu**
 
 
• Urdu is an Indo-Aryan language closely related to Hindi but written in the Perso-Arabic script.
 
• It is one of the 22 scheduled languages of India and serves as the official language of Jammu & Kashmir and Telangana.
 
• As per the 2011 Census, Urdu is spoken by approximately 5 crore (50 million) people in India.
 
• Urdu has a strong cultural and literary tradition, with notable poets such as Mirza Ghalib and Allama Iqbal contributing to its legacy.
 
 
 
• **Gujarati**
 
 
• Gujarati is an Indo-Aryan language spoken predominantly in the state of Gujarat.
 
• According to the 2011 Census, Gujarati is spoken by over 5 crore (50 million) people, making it one of the top 10 most spoken languages in India.
 
• It is the official language of Gujarat and has a rich literary tradition, with works by authors such as Narmad and Jhaverchand Meghani.
 
 
 
• **Kannada**
 
 
• Kannada is a Dravidian language spoken primarily in Karnataka.
 
• It is one of the scheduled languages of India and has a rich classical tradition, being designated as a "Classical Language" by the Government of India.
 
• Kannada is spoken by approximately 4 crore (40 million) people, as per the 2011 Census.
 
• Prominent Kannada literary figures include Kuvempu and Bendre.

questions.question: A sessions court, as per the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha (Second) Sanhita, 2023, is mandated to frame charges within _____ days from the first hearing on such charges.

__
 
• As per the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha (Second) Sanhita, 2023, sessions courts are required to frame charges within **sixty days** from the first hearing on such charges.
 
• This provision aims to ensure timely prosecution and prevent unnecessary delays in legal proceedings.
 
• The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, seeks to replace the colonial-era Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC) and modernize the judicial process in India.
 
• It focuses on transparency, accountability, and the expeditious handling of cases in order to strengthen the criminal justice system.
 
• The sixty-day timeframe underscores the importance of adhering to strict deadlines to enhance judicial efficiency and uphold justice.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Option 1: Fifteen days**

 
 
• Fifteen days is an insufficient time frame for framing charges in most sessions court cases, as it does not provide adequate time for legal review and preparation.
 
• This period is more commonly associated with preliminary procedures or remand orders in certain cases.
 
 
 
• **Option 2: Seventy-five days**
 
 
• Although seventy-five days could allow for more detailed case preparation, it exceeds the mandated sixty-day period specified in the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023.
 
• Such a delay could undermine the objective of expediting the judicial process.
 
 
 
• **Option 4: One hundred and twenty days**
 
 
• This period is significantly longer than necessary for framing charges in sessions court cases.
 
• Delays of this magnitude could lead to prolonged judicial processes and deny justice to victims and accused individuals alike.
 
 
 
• **Context of Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023**
 
 
• The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, is a comprehensive reform aimed at updating the criminal laws of India.
 
• It replaces outdated provisions in the CrPC to align with contemporary legal and social requirements.
 
• The reform emphasizes the protection of citizens' rights, timely delivery of justice, and reduced pendency of cases in courts.

questions.question: An astronaut with a mass of 60 kg lands on Mars. If Mars' gravitational acceleration is 3.7 m/s², what will be the astronaut's weight on Mars?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**222 N**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Weight is the force exerted by gravity on an object and is calculated using the formula **W = m × g**, where W is weight, m is mass, and g is gravitational acceleration.
 
• On Mars, the gravitational acceleration is **3.7 m/s²**, which is significantly lower than Earth's gravitational acceleration (9.8 m/s²).
 
• The astronaut's mass is given as **60 kg**. Using the formula, the weight on Mars is calculated as **W = 60 × 3.7 = 222 N**.
 
• Weight is measured in **Newtons (N)**, which is the SI unit for force.
 
• Gravitational acceleration varies across planets, impacting the weight of objects. For instance, on Earth, the astronaut's weight would be 588 N, higher than on Mars.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Option 2 (588 N):**

 
 
• This value represents the astronaut's weight on Earth, calculated using Earth's gravitational acceleration of 9.8 m/s².
 
• On Earth, the weight would be **W = 60 × 9.8 = 588 N**.
 
• Earth's gravitational force is higher compared to Mars, leading to a greater weight.
 
 
 
• **Option 3 (150 N):**
 
 
• This value does not correspond to the weight on Mars or any other planet in the solar system based on the given mass and gravitational acceleration.
 
• The calculation of weight depends strictly on the formula **W = m × g**, and 150 N could result from a lower gravitational acceleration on another celestial body.
 
 
 
• **Option 4 (360 N):**
 
 
• Similar to Option 3, this value does not align with the given data for Mars or Earth.
 
• It may represent an incorrect calculation or a hypothetical scenario with an intermediate gravitational acceleration.
 
 
 
• **Main Concept:**
 
 
• The weight of an object varies across celestial bodies due to differences in gravitational acceleration.
 
• Mass remains constant regardless of location, while weight is influenced by the gravitational force exerted by a planet.
 
• On planets with lower gravity like Mars, objects weigh less compared to their weight on Earth.

questions.question: The Nehru Report (1928) primarily recommended which of the following?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Dominion status and joint electorates**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Nehru Report was authored by **Motilal Nehru** in 1928 as a response to the challenge posed by the British government to draft a constitution for India.
 
• It recommended **Dominion Status** for India within the British Empire, rejecting the idea of complete independence at that time.
 
• The report advocated for **joint electorates**, opposing communal electorates to promote national unity and diminish divisions based on religion.
 
• It proposed a parliamentary system of governance with a bicameral legislature and guaranteed **fundamental rights**, including equality before the law and protection against discrimination.
 
• The report emphasized secularism, stating that **no state religion** would be imposed and all citizens would have equal rights irrespective of their religion.
 
• Although widely debated, the recommendations of the Nehru Report were rejected by the Muslim League, which demanded separate electorates and other safeguards for minorities.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

questions.question: The 'Vesara' architectural style, characterized by its unique combination of North and South Indian temple designs, predominantly developed in which region of India?
questions.solution:

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Vesara architectural style is a blend of Dravidian (South Indian) and Nagara (North Indian) styles of temple architecture.
 
• This style originated and flourished in the Deccan region, particularly under the patronage of the Chalukyas and the Hoysalas.
 
• The Chalukyas of Badami (6th to 8th century CE) were primarily responsible for the early development of the Vesara style, seen in their temples at Badami, Aihole, and Pattadakal.
 
• The Hoysalas (11th to 14th century CE) further enhanced this style, creating intricate and detailed carvings in temples like the Chennakesava Temple in Belur and the Hoysaleswara Temple in Halebidu.
 
• Vesara temples are characterized by their unique star-shaped ground plans, intricate carvings, and a combination of features from both the Dravidian and Nagara styles of architecture.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Central India:**

 
 
• Central India is known for its distinct temple architecture, such as the Khajuraho Group of Monuments in Madhya Pradesh, which exemplify the Nagara style.
 
• The temples are famous for their intricate sculptures and carvings, depicting various themes like mythology, everyday life, and erotica.
 
 
 
• **Northeast India:**
 
 
• The region has a unique architectural style influenced by its cultural and geographical diversity.
 
• Examples include the Kamakhya Temple in Assam, which reflects the Shakti cult and has a distinctively regional design.
 
• Unlike Vesara, temples in this region are not known for combining North and South Indian architectural features.
 
 
 
• **Eastern Coastal Plains:**
 
 
• The Eastern Coastal Plains, especially Odisha, are home to the Kalinga style of temple architecture, a sub-style of the Nagara tradition.
 
• Prominent examples include the Sun Temple at Konark and the Lingaraja Temple in Bhubaneswar.
 
• This style is characterized by curvilinear spires (Shikhara) and elaborate sculptures, distinct from the mixed approach of the Vesara style.
 
 
 
• **Vesara Architecture:**
 
 
• The term "Vesara" itself means "an intermediate" or "hybrid," highlighting its synthesis of the Dravidian and Nagara traditions.
 
• It represents the architectural innovation of the Deccan region, creating a distinct identity in Indian temple architecture.

questions.question: The defensive architecture of Rajput forts, such as Chittorgarh and Mehrangarh, is primarily characterized by which of the following features?

• Rajput forts, such as Chittorgarh and Mehrangarh, are renowned for their defensive architecture, designed to withstand prolonged sieges and invasions.
 
• Massive thick walls with bastions were integral to their construction, ensuring protection against cannon fire and enemy assaults.
 
• Bastions were strategically placed along the fort walls to allow soldiers to defend from elevated positions, providing a tactical advantage.
 
• The forts often used zigzagging pathways, narrow entrances, and high ramparts to confuse and slow down attackers.
 
• These architectural features highlight the military engineering expertise of the Rajput rulers and their emphasis on fortification as a defensive strategy.

• This feature is commonly associated with Mughal architecture, such as the Taj Mahal, rather than Rajput forts.

• It is primarily used to enhance the aesthetic appeal of palaces and tombs rather than defensive structures.
 
 
 
• **Vaulted ceilings with Romanesque designs**
 
 
• Vaulted ceilings and Romanesque designs are characteristic of European architecture, particularly seen in medieval churches and cathedrals.
 
• Rajput forts do not employ such features as their architectural style is rooted in Indian traditions and military needs.
 
 
 
• **Open courtyards and intricate lattice work**
 
 
• Open courtyards and lattice work (jalis) are indeed significant elements of Rajput architecture, particularly in palaces and havelis.
 
• However, these features serve aesthetic and functional purposes, such as ventilation and privacy, rather than defensive purposes.
 
• While prevalent in Rajput residential structures, they are not defining features of the defensive architecture of forts.

• In addition to massive fortifications, their forts often include temples, water reservoirs, and royal palaces.

questions.question: The "Basic Structure Doctrine," which limits Parliament's amending powers to prevent changes to the Constitution's essential features, was established in which landmark Supreme Court case?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Kesavananda Bharati**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The **Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973)** case is considered a landmark judgment by the Supreme Court of India.
 
• This case established the **"Basic Structure Doctrine"**, which limits Parliament's power to amend the Constitution in a way that alters its essential features.
 
• The judgment clarified that while Parliament has wide powers to amend the Constitution under Article 368, it cannot destroy or tamper with the fundamental framework or basic structure of the Constitution.
 
• The basic structure includes principles such as **separation of powers, fundamental rights, secularism, democracy**, and other essential elements.
 
• The ruling was delivered by a 13-judge bench, the largest bench ever constituted in the history of the Indian judiciary, and was decided by a thin majority of 7:6.
 
• This doctrine has since been pivotal in safeguarding constitutional integrity and protecting democratic values in India.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Minerva Mills v. Union of India (1980):**

 
 
• This case reinforced the Basic Structure Doctrine established in Kesavananda Bharati.
 
• The court struck down certain amendments to the Constitution, ruling that they violated the basic structure by curtailing judicial review powers.
 
• It emphasized the balance between fundamental rights and directive principles, stating that neither could override the other.
 
• The judgment further strengthened the doctrine by ensuring judicial scrutiny of constitutional amendments.
 
 
 
• **Indira Sawhney v. Union of India (1992):**
 
 
• Also known as the Mandal Commission case, it dealt with reservations for Other Backward Classes (OBCs) in government jobs and educational institutions.
 
• The Supreme Court upheld the 27% reservation for OBCs but introduced the concept of the "creamy layer," excluding economically advanced individuals within OBCs.
 
• This case focused on social justice and equality but did not involve the Basic Structure Doctrine.
 
 
 
• **A.K. Gopalan v. State of Madras (1950):**
 
 
• This case dealt with preventive detention laws and the interpretation of Article 21 (Right to Life and Personal Liberty).
 
• The Supreme Court ruled that the procedure established by law is sufficient to restrict personal liberty, limiting the scope of Article 21.
 
• However, this case was later overruled in **Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978)**, which expanded the interpretation of Article 21.
 
• This case did not address the Basic Structure Doctrine.
 
 
 
• **Basic Structure Doctrine:**
 
 
• The doctrine ensures that certain fundamental aspects of the Constitution, such as sovereignty, secularism, democracy, judicial independence, and fundamental rights, remain unaltered.
 
• It acts as a safeguard against arbitrary amendments that could undermine constitutional principles.
 
• The doctrine has been applied in multiple cases, including **Minerva Mills, Waman Rao, and S.R. Bommai**, to protect the Constitution's integrity.

questions.question: The technical term for the government's total income from all sources, including taxes, is ____________.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Government Revenue** refers to the total income collected by the government from all sources, including taxes, fees, fines, and grants.
 
• It is classified into two main categories: **Tax Revenue** (income from direct and indirect taxes) and **Non-Tax Revenue** (income from sources like dividends, interest, and user charges).
 
• This revenue is essential to fund public expenditures, including infrastructure projects, social schemes, defense, and administrative costs.
 
• Tax revenues are further divided into **direct taxes** (e.g., income tax, corporate tax) and **indirect taxes** (e.g., GST, customs duty).
 
• **Non-tax revenues** are generated from sources such as dividends from public sector enterprises, interest on loans given by the government, and income from public utilities.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Public Expenditure**

 
 
• It refers to the total spending by the government on various activities, including public services, infrastructure, defense, and welfare schemes.
 
• Public expenditure is categorized into **capital expenditure** (long-term investments like infrastructure) and **revenue expenditure** (day-to-day operational expenses like salaries and subsidies).
 
• It plays a crucial role in economic growth, employment generation, and poverty alleviation.
 
 
 
• **Fiscal Deficit**
 
 
• Fiscal deficit is the difference between the government's total expenditure and its total revenue, excluding borrowings.
 
• It indicates the amount of borrowing the government needs to meet its expenses.
 
• A high fiscal deficit may lead to inflation and increased public debt, while a low fiscal deficit indicates better fiscal discipline.
 
 
 
• **Capital Receipts**
 
 
• Capital receipts are funds received by the government through borrowings, disinvestment, or recovery of loans.
 
• These receipts are non-recurring in nature and are used primarily for capital expenditure.
 
• Examples include loans raised from domestic and foreign markets, sale of government assets, and repayment of loans by state governments or public enterprises.

questions.question: The process of breaking down dietary ______ into fatty acids and glycerol is essential for absorption in the human digestive system.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Fats**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The process of breaking down dietary **fats into fatty acids and glycerol** is known as **lipid digestion**.
 
• Digestion of fats begins in the small intestine with the help of bile secreted by the liver and lipase enzyme from the pancreas.
 
• Bile emulsifies fats into smaller droplets, while lipase breaks them down into **free fatty acids and monoglycerides**, making them absorbable by the intestinal cells.
 
• The digested fats are absorbed through intestinal villi and transported via the lymphatic system to the bloodstream as **chylomicrons**.
 
• Fats are a major source of **energy** for the body and play a critical role in cell membrane structure, hormone production, and vitamin absorption.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Starch**

 
 
• Starch is a carbohydrate that is broken down into **maltose and glucose** by the enzyme amylase during digestion.
 
• The digestion of starch begins in the mouth with salivary amylase and continues in the small intestine with pancreatic amylase.
 
• Glucose, the end product of starch digestion, is absorbed by the intestinal cells and used as a primary energy source by the body.
 
 
 
• **Peptides**
 
 
• Peptides are short chains of amino acids, which are the building blocks of proteins.
 
• Proteins are broken down into peptides and then into individual amino acids by enzymes like pepsin, trypsin, and chymotrypsin.
 
• Amino acids are absorbed in the small intestine and are essential for growth, repair, and various metabolic functions in the body.
 
 
 
• **RNA**
 
 
• RNA (Ribonucleic Acid) is a nucleic acid that plays a role in protein synthesis and various cellular processes.
 
• RNA is broken down into its basic components, nucleotides, during digestion by enzymes like ribonuclease.
 
• Unlike fats, RNA is not a significant dietary macronutrient but is ingested in small amounts from cellular materials in food.
 
 
 
• **About the digestive process of macronutrients**
 
 
• The human digestive system breaks down macronutrients (carbohydrates, proteins, and fats) into simpler forms for absorption.
 
• Each macronutrient has specific enzymes and processes for digestion, ensuring nutrients are efficiently absorbed and utilized by the body.
 
• Fats are digested differently from carbohydrates and proteins, requiring bile emulsification and enzymatic breakdown into fatty acids and glycerol.

questions.question: In the nervous system, neurons transmit signals. The part of a neuron primarily responsible for receiving incoming electrical signals from other neurons is the _______.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Dendrite**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Dendrites** are branch-like extensions of a neuron that receive electrical signals from other neurons or sensory stimuli.
 
• They are covered with synaptic receptors that allow them to communicate and transmit signals from the pre-synaptic neuron to the post-synaptic neuron.
 
• The primary function of dendrites is to collect and integrate incoming signals, which are then sent to the soma (cell body) for further processing.
 
• Dendrites increase the surface area of the neuron, enabling it to establish connections with multiple neurons and receive inputs from many sources.
 
• They play a critical role in synaptic plasticity, which is essential for learning and memory in the nervous system.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Axon terminal**

 
 
• The axon terminal is the endpoint of a neuron’s axon, where it communicates with other neurons, muscles, or glands.
 
• It releases neurotransmitters into the synaptic cleft to transmit signals to the next neuron or target cell.
 
• While it is involved in signal transmission, it does not receive incoming signals like dendrites do.
 
 
 
• **Soma**
 
 
• The soma, or cell body, is the central part of the neuron that contains the nucleus and organelles.
 
• It processes information received from the dendrites and generates an action potential if the threshold is reached.
 
• The soma is primarily responsible for maintaining the overall health and function of the neuron.
 
 
 
• **Nucleus**
 
 
• The nucleus is located within the soma and contains the neuron’s genetic material (DNA).
 
• Its primary function is to regulate gene expression and control the production of proteins essential for neuron function and repair.
 
• While it plays a vital role in maintaining cellular health, it is not directly involved in signal transmission or reception.
